title: Some say Ram, some Khuda
hook: some call Him Ram, some Khuda, some serve as Gusain, some as Allah (Ramkali M5, ang 885)

segments.voice: Yesterday, taatee vaao, and your line: in his refuge. Did you step into the shade for a breath before answering something sharp? Today, a shabad that walks through a whole street of neighbors. Day six hundred sixty-eight.

Sunrise in an old Punjabi market town. From one direction, the call to prayer. From another, temple bells and someone chanting Ram. A man walks toward the river to bathe; another unrolls a mat to bow. Two neighbors greet each other in different words for the same morning. Guru Arjan lived in streets like that. And in one shabad he simply looked around and listed what he saw, without telling anyone they were wrong. Today: some say Ram.
screen: `AN OLD MARKET TOWN AT SUNRISE.` → `BELLS, A CALL, A CHANT.` → `A SHABAD THAT LISTS WHAT IT SEES.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Raag Ramkali, on Ang eight eighty-five. It opens, in paraphrase: some say Ram, Ram; some say Khuda. Some serve Gusain, some Allah. Ram is a name Hindus use for God. Khuda is the Persian word Muslims in India used. Gusain, a Lord, a master, was used by Hindu devotees; Allah, the Arabic name, by Muslims. Then the refrain: He is the Cause of causes, the Generous One; He showers mercy, the Merciful. Notice the refrain's own words. Kareem and Raheem, generous and merciful, are Arabic names of God, used in Islam, here sung in a Sikh scripture. The shabad keeps going down the street. Some bathe at holy rivers, some go on Hajj. Some do puja, some bow their heads in prayer. Some read the Vedas, some the Kateb, the books Muslims revere. Some wear blue, some white. Some call themselves Hindu, some Muslim. Some ask for one paradise, some for another. It's a portrait of a neighborhood, drawn fairly. Then the last line turns. In paraphrase: Nanak says, whoever recognizes the Lord's hukam, the divine order, knows the Master's secret. The shabad doesn't say the names are all the same thing, or that the practices don't matter. It says that behind every name there's one Lord, and what counts is recognizing His will. It's a shabad for living alongside people who pray differently. In its view, a neighbor's word for God names the same One.
screen: `RAM, KHUDA, GUSAIN, ALLAH.` · `KAREEM AND RAHEEM IN THE REFRAIN.` · `A WHOLE STREET, DRAWN FAIRLY.` · `RECOGNIZE THE HUKAM.` · then, large: `MANY NAMES, ONE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor one name you don't use. Sit, and bring to mind a name for God that isn't the one you grew up with, or a name a friend or neighbor uses. Say it silently, once, with respect, the way you'd say a person's name you'd just learned. Then think of someone who prays with that name, and wish them well. If you pray, you can say Waheguru after it, and let the two names sit side by side. The bell holds the time.
Hukam, the divine order: Guru Arjan's shabad says some call the Lord Ram, some Khuda, some Gusain, some Allah, and the one who recognizes it knows His secret.
Your line: many names, one lord. Today, when you hear someone speak of God in words that aren't yours, listen for the One behind them. Day six hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing this shabad of Guru Arjan in kirtan, and often turn to it at interfaith gatherings as a picture of neighbors who name God differently.

it lists each practice fairly and turns to recognizing the hukam.
Arabic names of God appear in the refrain
kareem and raheem, generous and merciful, are sung in the Sikh scripture.

fork.setup: the shabad has listed Ram, Khuda, Hajj, puja, the Vedas and more. where does Guru Arjan end?
options: by naming which practice is best.
by saying whoever recognizes the Lord's hukam knows His secret.
by asking everyone to stop praying.
fork.reveal: the last line points past the names to the hukam: recognizing the Lord's will is the secret.

original.note: Gurmukhi: some say Ram, Ram; the shabad's opening words, Ramkali M5, Ang 885.

trapdoor: what you thought: the shabad says all religions are the same.
what it means: it names many ways of praying fairly, and says one Lord stands behind them all.
what a scholar hears: the refrain uses Arabic divine names, kareem and raheem, and the close turns on hukam, a key idea of the Granth.

sources.ref: Ramkali Mahalla 5 (koee bolai raam raam koee khudaae), Ang 885

notes: Shabad paraphrased line by line (Ram/Khuda, Gusain/Allah; kaaran karan kareem, kirpaa dhaar raheem; tirath/Hajj; puja/bowing; Vedas/Kateb; blue/white; Hindu/Turk; heaven names; the hukam close). Confirm order and wording; the script renders 'Turk' as 'Muslim'.
Glosses: Khuda as Persian, Gusain as 'a Lord, a master' used by Hindu devotees. Confirm.
Phrase 'a shabad for living alongside people who pray differently' is a description of how Sikhs often use it; confirm.
